items.title: Focus Question: What force causes a car to follow a curve in the road?

answer.html: A net force directed toward the center of the curve (the centripetal force). On a flat road it is supplied by the static friction of the road on the tires.

items.title: Figure 7 (Analyze): a motion diagram shows a toy car going around a circular track with velocity vectors that get longer at each position, while the radius stays the same. How can you tell from the diagram that the motion is not uniform?

answer.html: The position vectors all have the same length (fixed radius), but the velocity vectors have different lengths, so the speed is changing. Uniform circular motion needs both a fixed radius and a constant speed (equal-length velocity vectors, with only their direction changing).

items.title: Figure 9 (Predict): a stone whirled in a horizontal circle in a sling is released. How would its horizontal acceleration and horizontal velocity change?

body.html: Once the sling stops pulling (the tension is gone), no horizontal force acts (ignoring air), so the acceleration is zero and the velocity stays constant.

answer.html: The horizontal acceleration becomes zero, and the stone flies off in a straight line along the tangent with constant horizontal velocity equal to its speed at release (it then falls as a projectile).

items.title: Crosscutting Concept: Systems and System Models (centrifugal "force" on a bus passenger)

question.html: A bus turns right and a passenger feels pushed to the left against the window. Make a model that explains this without a centrifugal force. Model: Draw a top view of the bus turning right. The passenger's velocity would continue straight (tangent to the curve) by inertia. The window and seat push the passenger toward the center of the turn (the only real horizontal force). Relative to the bus the passenger seems to be pushed outward, but that is just inertia.

answer.html: The only horizontal force on the passenger is the window/seat force toward the center of the turn. The "outward push" is the passenger's tendency to keep moving straight (Newton's first law), not a real force, since no agent exerts it.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 12: a cyclist rounds a circular bend

question.html: A cyclist rides at 11 m/s around a bend of radius 32 m. Find the centripetal acceleration and the agent that exerts the centripetal force.

body.html: 𝑣= 11 m/s, 𝑟= 32 m. Find 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>.
Centripetal acceleration is 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟, directed toward the center of the bend.

answer.html: 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 3.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> toward the center of the bend. The centripetal force is exerted by the road, through the static friction on the tires.

check.html: About 0.4 of g is a hard but reasonable lean-and-turn for a cyclist.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 13: a jet turns at 245 m/s

question.html: What is the smallest radius of turn that keeps the centripetal acceleration at or below 4.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>? Give the answer in km.

body.html: 𝑣= 245 m/s, 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>≤4.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝑟<sub>min</sub> in km.
𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟, so 𝑟= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>; a smaller radius means a larger acceleration.

answer.html: 15 km

check.html: A very fast jet needs a wide, gentle turn; tens of kilometers across is typical.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 14: a child rides a playground carousel

question.html: A 62-kg child stands 2.8 m from the center of a carousel and moves at 3.4 m/s. Find the friction force needed to keep the child moving in the circle.

body.html: 𝑚= 62 kg, 𝑟= 2.8 m, 𝑣= 3.4 m/s. Find 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>.
Static friction between the child's shoes and the platform is the only horizontal force, so it supplies the centripetal force: 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟.

answer.html: about 2.6 × 10<sup>2</sup> N (260 N), directed toward the center of the carousel

check.html: About 0.42 of the child's weight (608 N); plausible, since a fast carousel makes you grip the rail.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 15: a ball on a string

question.html: A 24 g ball is swung in a horizontal circle on a string of length 0.85 m with a period of 0.74 s. Find the tension in the string.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.024 kg, 𝑟= 0.85 m, 𝑇= 0.74 s. Find the tension 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>.
The string's tension provides the centripetal force: 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>= 𝑚𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>, with 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>.

check.html: The acceleration is about 6.3 g, and for a 24-g ball the force (1.5 N) is about 6.3 times its weight (0.235 N), consistent.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 16 (Challenge): a car on a flat curve

question.html: A car travels at 18 m/s on a flat curve of radius 48 m. Find the centripetal acceleration and the minimum coefficient of static friction needed to stay on the road.

body.html: 𝑣= 18 m/s, 𝑟= 48 m. Find 𝑎<sup>𝑐</sup> and 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>.
On a flat road, static friction provides the centripetal force: 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑚𝑔≥𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟. The normal force equals 𝑚𝑔 because there is no vertical acceleration; the mass cancels.

answer.html: 𝑎<sup>𝑐</sup>= 6.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>; minimum 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.69

check.html: A value between 0.6 and 0.8 is reasonable for good tires on dry pavement, so this speed is near the limit.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 17: a toy airplane flies in a horizontal circle on a control line held by a pilot standing at the center

question.html: What is the direction of the airplane's acceleration, and what force causes it?

answer.html: It accelerates toward the center of the circle (centripetal acceleration), and the force that causes this is the tension in the control line.

check.html: The line can only pull, and it pulls the airplane inward along the line.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 18: riders pinned against the wall of a spinning cylinder ride

question.html: In this amusement ride the riders stand against the wall of a cylinder that spins about its vertical axis. What is the direction of the horizontal force on a rider, and what exerts it?

body.html: The riders move in a circle, so the net horizontal force on them points toward the axis of rotation. The agent is the wall of the cylinder.

answer.html: The force is directed inward, toward the axis of the cylinder, and is exerted by the wall pushing on the rider (normal force). Friction between the wall and the rider (upward) balances the rider's weight.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 19: letter to the editor on a driving website that says a car "is thrown outward by centrifugal force"

question.html: Write a short letter correcting the claim.

answer.html: Dear Editor: Your driving guide says that when a car rounds a bend, centrifugal force throws it toward the outside of the curve. This is wrong. There is no outward force acting on the car, because no object exerts one. The only horizontal force on the car is friction from the road, directed toward the center of the curve, and this net inward force (the centripetal force) causes the car's centripetal acceleration 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟. The car slides toward the outside only when the required centripetal force 𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟 is larger than the maximum static friction 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑚𝑔, which happens at high speed or on wet or icy pavement. The outward sensation is inertia: your body tends to continue in a straight line. Sincerely, A physics student.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 20: sitting in the back seat as the car goes around a curve to the left

question.html: Find (a) the direction of your acceleration, (b) the direction of the net force on you, and (c) what exerts that force. Diagram description: From above, the car curves left. The motion diagram shows velocity vectors tangent to the path, with the change in velocity 𝛥𝑣 pointing to the left (toward the center). The free- body diagram of you shows a horizontal force to the left (from the seat or door), plus gravity and the normal force from the seat that cancel vertically.

body.html: The acceleration points toward the center of the curve, and the net force points the same way as the acceleration.

answer.html: (a) to the left (toward the center of the curve) (b) to the left (toward the center) (c) the seat (friction) and the door of the car push on you; if you are leaning against the left-hand door, the door exerts the force.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 21: an object on a 0.95-m string makes one revolution in 1.4 s

question.html: Find its centripetal acceleration.

body.html: 𝑟= 0.95 m, 𝑇= 1.4 s. Find 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>.
𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: 19 m/s<sup>2</sup> toward the center of the circle

check.html: About 2 g, plausible for a quickly swung object.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 22: a 55.0-g stone whirled on a string

question.html: A 55.0 g stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string of length 0.85 m (measured from the hand to the stone) at a speed of 3.1 m/s. Find the tension in the string.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.0550 kg, 𝑣= 3.1 m/s, 𝑟= 0.85 m. Find the tension.
Tension provides the centripetal force: 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>= 𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟.

check.html: The stone's weight is 0.54 N, so a similar-sized tension is plausible.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 23: a carnival ride with 𝑟= 6.5 m and a period of 3.1 s

question.html: Find the rider's speed and centripetal acceleration.

body.html: 𝑟= 6.5 m, 𝑇= 3.1 s. Find 𝑣 and 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>.
In one period the rider travels the circumference: 𝑣= 2𝜋𝑟/ 𝑇, and 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: 𝑣= 13 m/s (tangent to the circle) and 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 27 m/s<sup>2</sup> toward the center (about 2.7 g)

check.html: 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟= (13.2)<sup>2</sup> / 6.5 = 27 m/s<sup>2</sup>, matching.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 24 (Critical Thinking): uniform circular motion from Earth's rotation at latitude 40.0° N

question.html: A 65.0-kg person stands on the ground at latitude 40.0° N. Earth's radius is 6.38 × 10<sup>6</sup> m and it turns once in 86 164 s. Which agent supplies the centripetal force, and what are the person's centripetal acceleration and the net force on the person?

body.html: At latitude 𝜑 the person moves in a circle of radius 𝑟= 𝑅cos𝜑 about Earth's axis, so a net force must point toward that axis. The agent is Earth's gravity: the part of gravity not balanced by the normal force supplies the centripetal force.

answer.html: The agent is Earth's gravitational force (the net of gravity and the normal force from the ground points toward Earth's axis). 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 0.0260 m/s<sup>2</sup> and the net force is about 1.7 N, which is only about 0.27% of the person's 637 N weight.

check.html: The effect is tiny because 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub> (0.026 m/s²) is much smaller than g (9.80 m/s²); it is zero at the poles and largest at the equator.

items.title: Focus Question: What force causes an object to move in a circle?

answer.html: A net force directed toward the center of the circle (the centripetal force), supplied by some real agent such as a string's tension, friction, gravity, or a normal force.

items.title: Figure 7 (Analyze): how can you tell from the diagram that the motion is uniform?

answer.html: The position vectors 𝑟<sub>1</sub> and 𝑟<sub>2</sub> have the same length (fixed radius) and the velocity vectors 𝑣<sub>1</sub> and 𝑣<sub>2</sub> have the same length (constant speed); only their directions change.

items.title: Figure 9 (Predict): how would the hammer's horizontal acceleration and velocity change if the thrower released the chain?

body.html: Once the chain's tension is gone, no horizontal force acts (ignoring air), so the acceleration is zero and the velocity stays constant.

answer.html: The horizontal acceleration becomes zero, and the hammer flies off in a straight line along the tangent with constant horizontal velocity equal to its speed at release (it then falls as a projectile).

items.title: Crosscutting Concept: Systems and System Models (centrifugal "force" in a turning car)

question.html: Model: Draw a top view of a car turning left. The passenger's velocity would continue straight (tangent to the curve) by inertia. The door pushes the passenger toward the center of the turn (the only real horizontal force). Relative to the car the passenger seems to be pushed outward, but that is just inertia.

answer.html: The only horizontal force on the passenger is the door/seat force toward the center. The "outward push" is the passenger's tendency to keep moving straight (Newton's first law), not a real force, since no agent exerts it.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 12: runner rounding a bend

question.html: A runner at 8.8 m/s rounds a bend of radius 25 m. Find the centripetal acceleration and the agent that exerts the centripetal force.

body.html: 𝑣= 8.8 m/s, 𝑟= 25 m. Find 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>.
Centripetal acceleration is 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟, directed toward the center of the bend.

answer.html: 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 3.1 m/s<sup>2</sup> toward the center of the bend. The centripetal force is exerted by the ground, through the static friction on the runner's shoes.

check.html: About a third of g is a modest acceleration for a runner.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 13: airplane turn at 201 m/s

question.html: Smallest radius that keeps 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub> below 5.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

body.html: 𝑣= 201 m/s, 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>≤5.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝑟<sub>min</sub> in km.
𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟, so 𝑟= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>; a smaller radius means a larger acceleration.

answer.html: 8.1 km

check.html: A fast plane needs a wide turn; several kilometers is typical.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 14: merry-go-round worker (Figure 10)

question.html: A 45-kg worker stands 6.3 m from the center and moves at 4.1 m/s. Find the friction force needed.

body.html: 𝑚= 45 kg, 𝑟= 6.3 m, 𝑣= 4.1 m/s. Find 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>.
Static friction between her feet and the platform is the only horizontal force, so it supplies the centripetal force: 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟.

answer.html: about 1.2 × 10<sup>2</sup> N (120 N), directed toward the center of the platform

check.html: About a quarter of her weight (441 N), plausible for a gentle ride.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 15: ball on a string, 16 g, 1.4 m, period 1.09 s

body.html: 𝑚= 0.016 kg, 𝑟= 1.4 m, 𝑇= 1.09 s. Find the tension 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>.
The string's tension provides the centripetal force: 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>= 𝑚𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>, with 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>.

check.html: The acceleration is about 4.7 g, and for a 16-g ball the force (0.74 N) is about 4.7 times its weight (0.157 N), consistent.

items.title: Lesson 2, Practice Problem 16 (Challenge): car on a flat curve

question.html: A car at 22 m/s on a curve of radius 56 m. Find 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub> and the minimum coefficient of static friction.

body.html: 𝑣= 22 m/s, 𝑟= 56 m. Find 𝑎<sup>𝑐</sup> and 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>.
On a flat road, static friction provides the centripetal force: 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑚𝑔≥𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟. The normal force equals 𝑚𝑔 because there is no vertical acceleration; the mass cancels.

answer.html: 𝑎<sup>𝑐</sup>= 8.6 m/s<sup>2</sup>; minimum 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.88

check.html: A value just below 1 is reasonable for good tires on dry pavement (racing tires).

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 17: ball on a rope swung in a horizontal circle

answer.html: It accelerates toward the center of the circle (centripetal acceleration), and the force that causes this is the tension in the rope.

check.html: The rope can only pull, and it pulls the ball inward along the rope.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 18: clothes in a spinning top-load washer

body.html: The clothes move in a circle, so the net force on them points toward the axis of rotation. The agent is the wall of the drum.

answer.html: The force is directed inward, toward the center of the drum, and is exerted by the wall of the drum pushing on the clothes (normal force). The water goes through the holes because the wall cannot push on it.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 19: letter to the editor on "balancing centripetal and centrifugal forces"

answer.html: Dear Editor: Your article says a driver must balance the centripetal and centrifugal forces to avoid skidding. This is wrong. There is no outward "centrifugal force" acting on the car, because no object exerts it. In a turn, the only horizontal force on the car is friction from the road (toward the center of the curve), and that net inward force is the centripetal force; it causes the car's centripetal acceleration 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟. The car skids when the required centripetal force 𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟 exceeds the maximum static friction 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑚𝑔, which happens if the driver goes too fast or the road is wet or icy. The outward feeling is inertia: your body tends to continue in a straight line. Sincerely, A physics student.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 20: sitting in the back seat as the car goes around a curve to the right

question.html: Diagram description: From above, the car curves right. The motion diagram shows velocity vectors tangent to the path, with the change in velocity 𝛥𝑣 pointing to the right (toward the center). The free-body diagram of you shows a horizontal force to the right (from the door or seat), plus gravity and the normal force from the seat that cancel vertically.

body.html: The acceleration points toward the center of the curve, and the net force points the same way as the acceleration.

answer.html: (a) to the right (toward the center of the curve) (b) to the right (toward the center) (c) the seat (friction) and door of the car push on you; for you leaning against the door, the door exerts the force.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 21: object on a 1.8-m string, one revolution in

body.html: 𝑟= 1.8 m, 𝑇= 2.2 s. Find 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>.
𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: 15 m/s<sup>2</sup> toward the center of the circle

check.html: About 1.5 g, plausible for a quickly swung object.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 22: 40.0-g stone in Figure 12

question.html: Figure 12 shows the string length (hand to stone) as 0.60 m, so 𝑟= 0.60 m. Speed 2.2 m/s.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.0400 kg, 𝑣= 2.2 m/s, 𝑟= 0.60 m. Find the tension.
Tension provides the centripetal force: 𝐹<sub>𝑇</sub>= 𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> / 𝑟.

check.html: Weight of the stone is 0.39 N, so a similar-sized tension is plausible.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 23: amusement-park ride, 𝑟= 4.0 m, period

body.html: 𝑟= 4.0 m, 𝑇= 1.7 s. Find 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub> and 𝑣.
In one period the rider travels the circumference: 𝑣= 2𝜋𝑟/ 𝑇, and 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: 𝑣= 15 m/s (tangent to the circle) and 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 55 m/s<sup>2</sup> toward the center (about 5.6 g)

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2), Problem 24 (Critical Thinking): uniform circular motion from Earth's rotation

body.html: You move in a circle with Earth, so a net force must point toward Earth's axis. The agent is Earth's gravity: the part of gravity not balanced by the normal force supplies the centripetal force. On a scale, the scale pushes up with 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔−𝑚𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub> (at the equator). Work (equator estimate): 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>= 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑅/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = 4𝜋<sup>2</sup>(6.38 × 10<sup>6</sup> m) / (86 164 s)<sup>2</sup> = 0.034 m/s<sup>2</sup>, which is 0.34% of g. Because the scale reads the normal force, the reading is smaller than 𝑚𝑔 by 𝑚𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub>.

answer.html: The agent is Earth's gravitational force (the net of gravity and the normal force from the ground or scale points toward Earth's axis). The motion slightly lowers the scale reading (your apparent weight), by about 0.3% at the equator and less at higher latitudes (none at the poles).

check.html: The effect is tiny because 𝑎<sub>𝑐</sub> (0.034 m/s²) is much smaller than g (9.8 m/s²).
